seo.title: Luigi Footprints Foundation | Community-led conservation in Kenya
seo.description: A Kenyan foundation protecting wildlife by empowering the communities who live alongside it: education, tree nurseries, women's enterprise and human-wildlife coexistence in the Amboseli ecosystem, Nairobi National Park and the Samburu National Reserve.

blocks.title: Protecting wildlife by empowering communities
blocks.subtitle: Community-led conservation in Kenya, from the Amboseli ecosystem to Nairobi National Park and the Samburu National Reserve.
blocks.content: In the heart of Kenya, where elephants still follow ancient migration routes and communities have lived alongside wildlife for generations, the future of people and nature is deeply connected. We believe conservation is not simply about protecting animals. It is about creating opportunity, restoring dignity, and giving communities the means to build sustainable futures. When communities thrive, wildlife thrives too.

image.alt: A herd of elephants walking among acacia trees, cattle egrets at their feet

blocks.title: What we believe
blocks.subtitle: Dignity for communities is equal to protection for wildlife.
blocks.content:
For too long, conservation has been treated as something separate from people's everyday lives. Our experience shows the opposite. The communities living closest to wildlife are not obstacles to conservation. They are its greatest partners.

When young people receive an education, they become the next conservation leaders. When women earn an income, families become more resilient. When landscapes are restored, wildlife and people both benefit. And when people feel included and respected, conservation lasts.

image.alt: Young volunteers planting mangrove seedlings at the Kenyan coast

seo.title: About | Luigi Francescon's legacy and our trustees
seo.description: The Luigi Footprints Foundation was founded in memory of Luigi Francescon. Read his story, what guides the foundation, and meet the Board of Trustees.

blocks.title: Our story
blocks.subtitle: Founded in memory of Luigi Francescon, whose love for Kenya, its wildlife and its people still guides the work.
blocks.content: Growing up near Nairobi National Park, Luigi knew a Kenya where wildlife moved freely across the landscape and nature was an everyday part of life. Those early years gave him a lifelong respect for the natural world and a deep concern for the wellbeing of the generations to come.

image.alt: Foundation members and supporters gathered beside a Walk for Elephants vehicle

blocks.title: The legacy
blocks.subtitle: He understood that conservation and human development are inseparable.
blocks.content:
Wildlife cannot survive if communities are struggling. Communities cannot thrive if the ecosystems they depend on are lost.

After Luigi's passing in 2016, the foundation was created to carry that understanding forward: protecting wildlife while creating opportunities for children, families and communities across Kenya. Today it works through practical, community-led programmes in the Amboseli ecosystem, Nairobi National Park and the Samburu National Reserve.

image.alt: Visitors and community members planting trees in Nairobi National Park

blocks.content: Protecting wildlife and uplifting communities were never opposing forces. They are two sides of the same footprint.
blocks.subtitle: Luigi Francescon, 1948–2016

image.alt: Portrait of Luigi Francescon

blocks.title: The elephant who carries the name
blocks.subtitle: A name given to a man, carried on by an elephant.
blocks.content:
In the Amboseli plains there is a young bull elephant called Luigi. He was named after Luigi Francescon, and he has been growing up alongside the foundation that carries the same name: born into the LD family, raised by his mother Lemlepo, and watched over by the communities and rangers we work with.

Luigi turned nine in May 2025, is ten now, and is growing up well. Lemlepo has raised a large and successful family of around forty elephants and has become a grandmother herself. Like all young bulls, Luigi spends his days sparring with other males, learning what he will need before he strikes out on his own. Across the Amboseli ecosystem, no poaching incident has been reported for several years.

He is not a mascot. He is a measure. As long as an elephant called Luigi can roam these plains safely, the work is doing what it was created to do.

image.alt: A herd of elephants walking among acacia trees, cattle egrets at their feet

items.title: Mission
items.description: To create thriving communities that take an active part in conserving wildlife and natural ecosystems, through education, economic empowerment, sustainable livelihoods and environmental stewardship.

items.title: Vision
items.description: A world where empowered communities and healthy ecosystems coexist, securing a sustainable future for the generations to come.

items.title: Philosophy
items.description: Dignity for communities is equal to protection for wildlife. When young people are educated, women earn an income and landscapes are restored, conservation becomes a natural, community-led choice.

blocks.title: Board of Trustees
blocks.subtitle: The people responsible for the foundation's governance and for its work on the ground.

items.name: Annabella Francescon
items.bio: For Annabella, wildlife conservation and youth engagement are lifelong callings. Growing up, she witnessed a raw, untouched Kenya when traveling between Nairobi and Mombasa meant going on a true dirt-track safari surrounded by thousands of migrating elephants. Mesmerized by these special creatures, elephants became her emblem animal, sparking decades of dedicated support for the survival of elephants, rhinos, and African wildlife. Alongside her environmental focus, Annabella finds immense joy in working with young people, firmly believing that the future belongs to their exuberance. She is passionately committed to providing youth with the formal and practical education they need to confidently navigate the world ahead.

image.alt: Annabella Francescon, Chairman

items.name: Peter Mwangi Karanja
items.bio: Born and raised in Loitokitok on the picturesque slopes of Mt. Kilimanjaro, Peter has spent his entire life alongside the spectacular wildlife of Amboseli National Park and Tsavo West. His journey began as an active member of the Wildlife Clubs of Kenya, which paved the way for a fulfilling career in the tourism industry. Over the years, working with renowned conservationists like Annabella, Pat Awori, Cynthia Moss, and Jonathan Scott deepened his appreciation for our planet's irreplaceable habitats. Having stood on the frontlines against the poaching crises of the 1990s and 2000s, Peter believes collective action can overcome any threat. Today, alarmed by the destruction of local forests, he channels his urgency into aggressive tree-planting initiatives, helping the foundation restore ecosystems little by little. As the Swahili saying goes, 'Kidogo Kidogo Hujaza Kibaba.'

image.alt: Peter Mwangi Karanja, Secretary

items.name: Jose Manuel Lapena Casamayor
items.bio: Years ago, Jose Manuel traveled to Kenya for the first time with Annabella as his guide. That transformative trip introduced him to a pristine, natural world thriving in close proximity to the wildlife he had always dreamed of experiencing. From that exact moment, he realized the urgent global responsibility to preserve these wild landscapes for future generations. Having returned to Africa numerous times since, that initial feeling has only grown stronger, driving his unwavering commitment to leverage his financial oversight skills to support and conserve our natural planet.

image.alt: Jose Manuel Lapena Casamayor, Treasurer

items.name: Daniel Muturi Gatumbo
items.bio: Daniel's path to conservation came through a gradual, powerful awareness of how human actions can inadvertently harm our planet. As a primary school student, he loved the hands-on responsibility of planting trees and grass to heal bare, eroded hillsides. Haunted by childhood stories of extinct creatures like dinosaurs, he often wondered what would happen if mankind turned the world into a barren desert. This early curiosity evolved into a professional mission when he entered the tourism industry, realizing that his livelihood, and the livelihood of his community, is entirely dependent on keeping Kenya's natural scenery and wildlife safe, vibrant, and accessible.

image.alt: Daniel Muturi Gatumbo, Operations Coordinator

items.name: Justin Chuma Kenya
items.bio: Raised on the lush, green slopes of Mount Kenya, Chuma watched with a heavy heart as domestic and commercial deforestation stripped away over fifty percent of his childhood landscape. Refusing to remain a bystander, he joined environmental clubs throughout his school and college years to restore the natural beauty he remembered. His deep passion for indigenous trees led him to mobilize local communities and authorities to plant more trees than were being lost. Today, Chuma uses his accounting expertise to ensure the foundation's resources are perfectly balanced to combat the real-world threats of global warming and environmental degradation.

image.alt: Justin Chuma Kenya, Accountant

seo.title: Our work | Education, restoration, enterprise and coexistence
seo.description: Four programmes in Kenya: scholarships and the Amboseli OYC Choir, the Olchani tree nurseries, Dignity Tailors and Maasai beadwork enterprise, and coexistence tools including Dignity Housing for rangers.

blocks.title: Our work
blocks.subtitle: Practical, community-led programmes in the Amboseli ecosystem, Nairobi National Park and the Samburu National Reserve.
blocks.content: We work face to face with the people who live alongside wildlife, designing programmes that answer the real, everyday challenges of doing so, and making sure conservation brings tangible social and economic value.

image.alt: Volunteers with collection bags during a clean-up at Lake Nakuru National Park

blocks.title: Education and youth
blocks.subtitle: Educating the next generation of conservation leaders.
blocks.content:
The future of conservation depends on the young people who will inherit it. Across the Amboseli ecosystem we fund secondary school scholarships and run conservation workshops, mentorship and environmental awareness programmes that help young people understand their role in protecting the world around them. Our programmes have reached thousands of students so far.

The Amboseli OYC Choir is one of the most inspiring. Young people use music, dance and poetry to carry messages of conservation, culture and coexistence into their own communities.

image.alt: Students sitting an exam in a Kenyan classroom

blocks.title: Landscape restoration
blocks.subtitle: The Olchani Project: restoring landscapes, one tree at a time.
blocks.content:
Healthy ecosystems support healthy communities. Through the Olchani Project, funded and run in partnership with ifaw, we restore degraded land, strengthen wildlife corridors and help communities become stewards of their own environment. Olchani means tree in the Maa language.

Tree planting is not simply putting seedlings in the ground. It rebuilds ecosystems, improves climate resilience and creates livelihoods. Working with local communities, we have established four community-managed nurseries with capacity for 42,000 indigenous seedlings, among them Osoit, Ildepen and Tembo, creating work and skills for women and young people. Their seedlings go to restoration sites such as the Orregie Enclosure inside Amboseli National Park, planned as a forest of 5,000 to 7,000 indigenous trees.

image.alt: Indigenous seedlings being unloaded for a community planting day

blocks.title: Community enterprise
blocks.subtitle: Creating opportunities for the people who live with wildlife.
blocks.content:
Conservation succeeds when families can see its benefits in daily life. The Dignity Tailors programme gives women skills training, craftsmanship and a route into business. The Inkaramatak Ildepen Maasai Ushanga shop lets Maasai women sell their beadwork directly to travellers and keep the value of their work. Tourism partnerships invite visitors to take part in conservation activities while supporting local livelihoods.

Stronger household incomes make communities active partners in protecting wildlife and the land it depends on.

image.alt: A farmer harvesting cabbages during the COVID-19 livelihoods project

blocks.title: Coexistence and guarding
blocks.subtitle: Helping people and wildlife share the same land, and supporting the rangers who protect it.
blocks.content:
For communities near protected areas, encounters with predators and elephants can threaten livestock, crops and lives. Rather than choose between people and wildlife, we work on solutions that serve both: predator-deterrent lighting that protects homesteads, beekeeping that earns an income while discouraging elephants from entering settlements, and coexistence training for the community leaders who hold it all together.

Behind every protected landscape are rangers who spend long periods away from home in remote conditions. Through the Dignity Housing project we are replacing tents with safe, self-contained homes for rangers in Amboseli, Nairobi National Park and Samburu National Reserve. Six of Nairobi's 25 ranger camps have been housed so far, and an eight-unit base opened at Samburu in early 2026.

image.alt: Trustee Annabella Francescon inside a completed Dignity House for rangers

blocks.subtitle: In short
blocks.content: Four programmes, one approach. Scholarships and the Amboseli OYC Choir keep young people in school and give them a voice. The Olchani Project puts restoration in local hands, with four community-run nurseries for 42,000 indigenous seedlings. Dignity Tailors and the Maasai Ushanga shop turn craft into income that stays at home, and lighting, beekeeping and Dignity Housing make it safer to live alongside wildlife. None of it is done for communities. All of it is done with them.

projects.title: Olchani Project
projects.excerpt: Olchani means tree in the Maa language. It began with one nursery in Amboseli in 2021 and has become a way of life: communities growing indigenous trees, and earning a dignified living doing it.
projects.content:
Olchani is the Maa word for tree, and the project does what its name says. It grows indigenous trees across the Amboseli ecosystem, and the people who do the work are paid for it, own it and keep it going.

It started in May 2021 with a location and a promise. Dr Winnie Kiiru offered her place in the Amboseli area to host the first tree nursery, and Jim Nyamu agreed to help care for the seedlings. Four trees went into the ground to inaugurate it, and the invitation was open to anyone who wanted to help reforest the ecosystem, for the elephants and giraffe that live in it and for the clean air of the people who live there too.

From that beginning the work became communal. Nurseries were established with youth at the Kenya Wildlife Service’s Amboseli headquarters and at Oldoinyo Oibor Primary School, and then in the communities themselves. The first was the Osoit nursery, Intomonok Osoit, built for ten thousand seedlings, and the Ildepen and Tembo nurseries followed. Local women, the mamas, raise the seedlings and earn a real income for it. Decisions are made in barazas, the community meetings where everyone with a stake in the land has a voice.

The seedlings are planted out into restoration sites, chief among them the Orregie Enclosure inside Amboseli National Park. It is planned as a small forest of five to seven thousand indigenous trees, and it helps hold a wildlife corridor open. On National Tree Planting Day the community put four hundred seedlings into the ground there in a single day. Beyond the restoration sites, the project carries tree-growing into households, churches and schools, putting seedlings directly into families’ hands.

The partnership with ifaw has grown alongside it; when ifaw marked twenty-five years of conservation work in East Africa, its team planted trees raised in these community nurseries. And the thinking has extended beyond trees: Olchani’s second phase added grass and fodder, and became Ubuntu Hay, the community hay bank at Lemongo.

In the foundation’s own words, restoration is more than planting trees. It is mamas leading community nurseries and earning dignified incomes, youth growing trees while growing their purpose, and communities healing land while healing livelihoods.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: the mamas of a community nursery in the Amboseli ecosystem raising indigenous seedlings.

projects.title: Ubuntu Hay
projects.excerpt: A community-owned hay bank at Lemongo, near Amboseli, that stores fodder in the good seasons so that livestock, livelihoods and grasslands come through drought.
projects.content:
Drought is the hardest season for families who keep livestock alongside wildlife. Ubuntu Hay, the second phase of the Olchani Project, answers it with foresight: community members harvest grass, bale it and fill a community hay barn built with them and for them, so there is feed in store when the rains are late or fail.

Stored fodder means livestock can be kept through a dry season without stripping the grasslands that wildlife depends on, and it gives families a buffer that protects their animals and their income. Women, men and young people run the hay bank themselves, with ifaw as partner, and its chairman, John, leads the work on the ground.

Ubuntu Hay launched in mid-2025, and the community carried out its first harvest and baling in September that year. The foundation describes it as climate resilience stored for tomorrow and economic empowerment created today.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: the community baling hay at the Lemongo hay bank, from the foundation's Ubuntu Hay in Action post of September 2025.

projects.title: Ubuntu Smiles
projects.excerpt: Women's economic empowerment in the Amboseli ecosystem: dignified incomes from beadwork, crafts and the community tree nurseries, and with them a measure of independence.
projects.content:
Ubuntu Smiles is the foundation's women's economic empowerment work in the Amboseli ecosystem. It supports women to earn from their skills, through beadwork and crafts and through the community nurseries they run, and connects that income to a wider sense of dignity and possibility.

It runs alongside the Olchani restoration work, with ifaw as partner. The women who have taken part describe it in their own words: community leader Anna Touwa has spoken about the economic empowerment it brought to her life and to other women in her community.

The craft and income work runs through the foundation's story, from early value-addition sessions with Amboseli women, to beadwork, to the named Ubuntu Smiles programme profiled in 2025. When women earn, families become more resilient and communities become stronger partners for wildlife.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: Anna Touwa speaking about Ubuntu Smiles, from the foundation's Gratitude, Dignity, and the Power of Ubuntu post of November 2025.

projects.title: Outdoor Classroom Series
projects.excerpt: Conservation lessons for primary school children at the community tree nurseries in Amboseli, led by the community leaders who live the work every day.
projects.content:
The Outdoor Classroom Series takes conservation education out of the classroom and into the nurseries and the soil. Children from nearby primary schools come to the foundation's community-led tree nurseries for hands-on sessions on indigenous trees, restoration and living alongside wildlife.

The lessons are led not only by teachers but by community coexistence leaders: Anna Touwa at the Ildepen nursery, in a session the foundation called Learning Beyond the Classroom, and Nickson Seleon at the Osoit nursery, in Learning by Living It. Both ran in early 2026.

The series sits within the Olchani Project, with ifaw and Stand Up Shout Out as partners. The aim is a generation that has experienced conservation rather than only been told about it. In the foundation's words, education is not just something you are taught, it is something you experience.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: children at a conservation session in the Osoit nursery, from the foundation's Outdoor Classroom Series post of 17 February 2026.

projects.title: Nanare Art Challenge
projects.excerpt: An immersive leadership experience built around art for thirty teenagers from Kakamega, run with Stand Up Shout Out at the SUSO Mabingwa Youth Centre.
projects.content:
Sometimes empowerment looks like a paintbrush. The Nanare Art Challenge placed paint, fabric and possibility in front of thirty young people from Kakamega, many of whom had never drawn before, and invited them to create.

Run in partnership with Stand Up Shout Out at the SUSO Mabingwa Youth Centre in Nairobi, and led by SUSO's founder Peter Fredrick Moll with SUSO staff and youth leaders as facilitators, it grew over several days into far more than an art competition: a journey of leadership, collaboration and self-discovery.

By the end, the foundation reports, all thirty participants said they felt more confident, more exposed to new possibility and more like changemakers. It built on earlier art days the foundation has hosted with visiting artists, including one with young people in Kibera.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: teenagers painting at the SUSO Mabingwa Youth Centre, from the foundation's Something beautiful began post of September 2026.

projects.title: Living Safely With Wildlife
projects.excerpt: Coexistence training that equips community ambassadors, including women leaders, with the knowledge and tools to live safely alongside wildlife and reduce conflict.
projects.content:
For communities who live beside wildlife every day, coexistence is a practical skill. The foundation supports toolbox trainings that give community ambassadors the knowledge and tools to live safely alongside wildlife and to reduce conflict before it costs lives, livestock or crops.

In 2025 the foundation co-sponsored a human-wildlife coexistence toolbox training led by Save the Elephants, bringing together community representatives from the Amboseli and Nairobi National Park areas with youth from Stand Up Shout Out. In 2026, at its Living Safely With Wildlife training in Samburu, women leaders from the SUSO coexistence villages stepped forward to ask questions, share lived experience and learn new approaches and technologies.

The foundation's account of the Samburu training is direct: you don't just train a woman, you strengthen a leader, one who carries that knowledge home to her family, her village and the next generation.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: women leaders standing to speak at the Samburu training, from the foundation's When Women Stand Up post of 2026.

projects.title: Mazingira Day at Nairobi National Park
projects.excerpt: More than a hundred young volunteers clearing invasive Parthenium weed from the grasslands of Nairobi National Park on Mazingira Day 2025, with Stand Up Shout Out and the Kenya Wildlife Service.
projects.content:
Parthenium is an invasive weed that chokes the grasslands wildlife grazes. On Mazingira Day in October 2025, more than a hundred young volunteers joined the foundation, Stand Up Shout Out and the Kenya Wildlife Service in Nairobi National Park to clear it by hand.

The day is part of a longer commitment to youth in conservation, in which young changemakers restore parks, plant and tend trees, and pass what they learn on to the children coming up behind them, supported with the tools and refreshments the work needs.

It continues work the foundation began years earlier: an earlier Parthenium clearance at the park is one of the oldest entries in this archive. Conservation lasts when young people own it.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: young volunteers in vests clearing Parthenium in Nairobi National Park, from the foundation's Mazingira Day post of 11 October 2025.

projects.title: The Elephant Den
projects.excerpt: A summit where young people from five Kenyan counties pitched real businesses for a grant to start them, so that conservation’s next generation got capital as well as advice.
projects.content:
Young people who live alongside wildlife need a living that does not come at wildlife’s expense. The foundation’s answer was The Elephant Den, TED for short: a competition with money at the end of it rather than one more workshop.

In March 2022 the foundation and Stand Up Shout Out brought five groups of young Kenyans together at the SUSO headquarters, where they camped for the summit. They came from Nakuru, Amboseli, Taita Taveta, Embu and Nairobi, and each group presented a commercial business built for the place they actually live, competing for a grant to start it. A panel of four heard them out: Peter Karanja and Annabella Francescon for the foundation, and Peter Moll and Poebe for SUSO. The panel gave advice aimed at turning the ideas into working enterprises. The proposals were, in the foundation’s words, impressive and well thought out for the areas they come from.

It did not end at the pitch. The following month the foundation handed four acres of land near Embu town to SUSO’s chief executive Peter Moll and the Embu County Director, to be set up as a tree nursery and a base for other agricultural work. The result is a commercial venture for young people that is also good for the land it sits on.

The foundation described TED at the time as a new chapter: empowering youth into the future with commercial enterprises for their own livelihoods. The idea behind it runs through everything the foundation has built since: conservation holds when the people nearest to wildlife have something to gain from it.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: the five groups presenting at The Elephant Den summit, from the foundation's March 2022 post.

projects.title: Walk for Elephants with Jim Nyamu
projects.excerpt: Since Jim Nyamu's first walk in 2013, the foundation has walked every one of them with him, carrying the message that ivory belongs to elephants across Kenya and far beyond it.
projects.content:
Jim Nyamu walks. Since 2013, when he set out from Mombasa and covered 1,500 kilometres to put the plight of the elephant in front of the people who live alongside them, he has crossed Kenya and much of East Africa on foot under one banner: Ivory Belongs to Elephants. The foundation took the first steps of that first walk with him, and has joined every walk since.

What that support looks like is practical. The team flags Jim off at the start, walks stretches of the route beside him, stops with him to talk to communities along the way about their part in protecting elephants, and is waiting at the finish. In August 2021 the foundation walked the last stretch into Amboseli so that Jim arrived for World Elephant Day on the twelfth. That November, as he set out through the Great Rift Valley, the walk carried 10,000 trees to be planted along the route, and 3,500 of them were seedlings from the foundation.

The walks have grown longer. In July 2023 the foundation was at the flag-off of Jim's East and Central Africa walk through Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo, and travelled to the Malaba border to see the team across. In October 2024 the Horn of Africa Elephant Campaign Walk ended on its eighty-sixth day with the ceremonial handover of the Kenyan flag at the foundation, where Managing Director Peter Karanja and the team welcomed the walkers home. In April 2022, when Jim received the Presidential Order of the Grand Warrior, the award ceremony was held in the foundation's own garden.

projects.title: Sponsoring exams
projects.excerpt: Standing behind students through the examinations that decide where they go next, and staying in their lives long enough to see the results come in.
projects.content:
In Kenya a national examination decides a child’s next school, and with it a great deal of what follows. The foundation backs students through that moment: the years of schooling before it, the sitting of the examinations themselves, and the place the results earn.

The support is personal rather than administrative. The foundation has followed individual students through the Stand Up Shout Out network for years. Among the earliest were Brenda and Faith, whom the team took to the cinema in Nairobi in 2019 with their SUSO mentor Yvonne to mark how well they were doing at school. Staying close enough to know how a child is doing is what makes it possible to step in at the point where money, not ability, would otherwise decide the outcome.

Where strong results open a door, the foundation’s scholarship programme carries the student through it.

featuredImage.altText: Students sitting an exam in a Kenyan classroom

projects.title: Scholarships
projects.excerpt: Full secondary-school scholarships for young people whose examination results have earned them a place they could not otherwise take up, awarded with Stand Up Shout Out.
projects.content:
A strong national examination result opens the door to a good secondary school. The cost of that school closes it again for families who cannot pay. The foundation’s scholarship programme exists for exactly that gap.

The scholarships are awarded together with Stand Up Shout Out, to young people already being mentored through SUSO’s programmes, and they are full scholarships, decided on the strength of KCPE results, of talent, and of what the student has already put back into their community. They are awarded for who a young person is becoming, not only for a mark on a paper.

In 2022 three young women from Kibra and Dagoretti, all of them from SUSO’s Own Your Crown programme for women and girls’ leadership, won full scholarships on their KCPE results and enrolled in excellent Kenyan high schools: Sarah, Hope and Fantasia. They reported for Form 1 that May.

The foundation and SUSO say the scholarships carry more than an education: character and leadership development, and a commitment to walk with each young leader the whole way. The aim is a strong, resilient community, built by people who were raised inside it and chose to stay and lift it.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: the three Own Your Crown scholarship recipients, from the foundation's May 2022 posts.

projects.title: Providing water to wildlife in Kenya's national parks
projects.excerpt: When the dry season empties the waterholes, the foundation hires bowsers and fills them. On one World Elephant Day alone, that meant 88,000 litres into Tsavo East.
projects.content:
Kenya's dry seasons decide which animals live. Waterholes shrink to cracked mud, troughs run empty, and wildlife walks further and further for a drink, often into conflict with people. Where a park cannot hold water through a drought, the foundation trucks it in.

On World Elephant Day in August 2020 the foundation hired seven bowsers carrying 88,000 litres into Tsavo East, where Kenya's largest elephant population lives, and used them to fill three waterholes, a mud pit and three water troughs. Thirty young people from Stand Up Shout Out travelled from Nairobi to Voi to do the work, on a day that also fell on Youth Day, with the Kenya Wildlife Service providing collaboration and security. In September 2021 the foundation returned to Tsavo with eight bowsers and 96,000 litres, filling troughs and a waterhole that had dried out completely.

The hardest test came with the drought of early 2023, in Nairobi National Park. For two months the foundation worked in a coalition with Friends of Nairobi National Park, BAPS Charity, the PKF Foundation and SUSO, with the Kenya Wildlife Service facilitating, to keep water and fodder going into the park. One March delivery alone brought 77,000 litres of water and 450 bales of hay, and the final run filled a desilted dam just before the rains arrived. Over those two months the coalition, backed by a long list of individual donors, delivered 1.2 million litres of water, 2,064 bales of hay and 203 bales of lucerne into the park. The figure belongs to all of them together; the foundation was one part of it.

featuredImage.altText: Water trucks delivering emergency water across dry, cracked ground during drought

projects.title: Planting mangroves at the coast
projects.excerpt: Mangroves are the only trees on earth built to live between land and sea. At Kenya's coast the foundation backs Stand Up Shout Out's Adopt A Creek programme, which has put tens of thousands of them back into the mud.
projects.content:
Mangroves grow where the tide meets the shore, rooted in salt and mud, and they hold the coast together: they break the force of waves before those waves reach a village, they trap the sediment that would otherwise wash the shoreline away, they store several times more carbon than most forests on land, and their tangled roots are the nursery for much of the fish the coast lives on. Kenya has been losing them.

The planting is run by Stand Up Shout Out, the youth organisation the foundation has worked alongside since the beginning, through its Adopt A Creek programme, and the foundation supports it. The work is concentrated in the creeks around Mombasa, at Jomvu Kuu and Tudor Creek, where more than ten thousand mangrove seedlings have been planted since 2021, chiefly Rhizophora mucronata and Avicennia marina, the species that do best in those waters. The Jomvu Kuu work is a partnership with the Bidii Creek Community Conservation group.

Planting is only half of it; the seedlings have to be raised first. The programme runs coastal nurseries. Five thousand mangroves were nursed at Jomvu Kuu and Tudor Creek, one nursery has grown to more than ten thousand seedlings, and the work has spread along the coastline from Kwale to Kilifi. On Wasini Island on the south coast it was extended with Shimoni Turtle Watch and the Wasini Women Group, who set up a village nursery of just over a thousand Ceriops tagal seedlings.

What makes it hold is who does it. The nurseries belong to the women’s groups and community conservation groups that run them, and the young people who plant the seedlings are from the villages the mangroves protect. The conservation work improves their livelihoods, and the hands in the mud belong to people from this coast.

featuredImage.altText: Photograph to come: young volunteers planting mangrove seedlings in tidal mud at Jomvu Kuu or Tudor Creek, from the Adopt A Creek posts.

projects.title: Gifting boots to game rangers
projects.excerpt: Rangers walk for a living. At a rhino ceremony with KWS at Lake Nakuru, the foundation gave them boots, and it has kept asking what else they need.
projects.content:
A ranger's job is walking. Patrols cover long distances over rough, wet, thorned ground, day after day, and boots wear out faster than they are replaced. In September 2020, at a rhino ceremony held with the Kenya Wildlife Service at Lake Nakuru National Park, the foundation and the Stand Up Shout Out team handed boots to the rangers there, to make the work possible and to thank them for keeping the park's rhinos, and all its wildlife, safe.

The gesture came out of time spent alongside them. Through the foundation's many days of clean-up work in Nairobi National Park, rangers led the volunteers, kept them safe and worked beside them, while their colleagues stayed out on the patrols that protect the park's rhinos. That watch has kept the sanctuary free of rhino poaching for over seven years. What rangers need is best learned from rangers, and the foundation has kept asking.

The answers have shaped everything since. In June 2022, twenty Kenya Wildlife Service rangers were honoured at Nairobi National Park and given twenty powerful rechargeable torches, which they had specifically asked for to strengthen their night operations. The same instinct, followed further, became the foundation's Dignity Housing Project.

featuredImage.altText: Pairs of new ranger boots laid out on a table for handover

projects.title: Cleaning Lake Nakuru National Park
projects.excerpt: A working trip to one of Kenya's great lake parks, spent on the ground with the Stand Up Shout Out youth team and the rangers who look after it.
projects.content:
Lake Nakuru National Park is a fenced sanctuary around an alkaline lake in the Rift Valley, famous for its flamingos and important as a stronghold for rhino. Keeping a park like it in good condition is unglamorous, physical work, and in September 2020 the foundation took a team there to do it, alongside young volunteers from Stand Up Shout Out.

The trip ran over several days. Between spells of work the team spent time with SUSO seeing the wildlife their activities were meant to help, and the visit closed with a rhino ceremony held with the Kenya Wildlife Service, at which the foundation handed boots to the park's rangers in thanks for their work protecting its rhinos.

featuredImage.altText: Volunteers with collection bags during a clean-up at Lake Nakuru National Park

projects.title: Sustaining community livelihoods during COVID-19
projects.excerpt: When the pandemic closed Kenya's schools and emptied its hotels, the foundation ran a weekly distribution into Kibra that reached 500 families, around 3,000 people, week after week.
projects.content:
COVID-19 hit hardest where people earn a daily wage. In Kibra, one of Nairobi's largest informal settlements, work disappeared almost overnight, and with schools closed the children lost their classrooms too. In April 2020 the foundation began funding a weekly distribution of food and books there, run with Maniago Safaris and the Stand Up Shout Out network led by Peter Moll, reaching 500 families, around 3,000 people.

It was run carefully. Fresh vegetables and fruit were sourced directly from nearby farms; a screening system controlled entry to the distribution centre; masks were compulsory and special overalls were made to keep the distributors safe. Beyond the food, the team sprayed matatus and boda bodas to keep the vehicles hygienic, and set up large buckets of water with taps, kept refilled, so that people passing by could wash their hands.

Education ran alongside it. The fourth distribution focused on schooling: 431 children received education packages designed by their own teachers, so they could study at home and hand work back to be marked. There were no computers involved. Every package was assembled and every book carried by hand, and teachers went back to the closed schools to collect and return the children's work.

The work spread beyond Kibra. Food was driven out to communities near the Maasai Mara whose livelihoods had collapsed with tourism. By July 2020 the programme had reached its tenth distribution and thousands of recipients. That September it turned from relief to repair: with the SUSO team, the foundation backed a Community Challenge that cleaned, painted and built pathways at the Phoenix Library and Three Bells Primary School, and began a green space beside the library that the young people named Little Karura.

featuredImage.altText: A farmer harvesting cabbages during the COVID-19 livelihoods project

projects.title: Eradicating the invasive Parthenium weed
projects.excerpt: Parthenium chokes the grasslands of Nairobi National Park. The foundation put 130 people to work pulling it out, and paid them, in a year when work had vanished.
projects.content:
Parthenium is an invasive weed that spreads fast through open grassland, crowding out the grasses that grazing wildlife depends on. It had begun to take hold in Nairobi National Park, and the only reliable way to remove it is by hand.

In June 2020 the foundation sponsored an operation to do exactly that. A hundred and thirty people went into the park to uproot the weed: the Maniago team, young volunteers from Stand Up Shout Out and residents of the Kibera settlement. Kenya Wildlife Service rangers protected them throughout, and the exercise was repeated twice a week over the following months.

It did two jobs at once. The work paid a small wage at a moment when the pandemic had wiped out livelihoods, and it took people into a park on their own doorstep that most of them had never been inside. They saw lions, rhino, giraffe and antelope in the course of a working day. Kenyan guides who had lost their own work joined the effort too, among them four of Maniago's own.

The removals have continued as a partnership. On World Environment Day in June 2022, SUSO, Maniago Safaris and the Kenya Wildlife Service cleared the murram pits between points 8 and 9 in the park, pulling out 611 kilogrammes of parthenium with more than eighty participants on the day.

featuredImage.altText: Volunteers in red shirts uprooting Parthenium weed in open grassland

projects.title: Tree planting at Nairobi National Park
projects.excerpt: Five hundred trees planted in the park on the city's doorstep, in holes the young volunteers dug themselves.
projects.content:
Nairobi is the only capital city in the world with a national park inside its limits, and keeping that park alive is a civic as much as a conservation task. In October 2021 the foundation and the youth of Stand Up Shout Out spent days in the park digging the holes, the hard physical part of tree planting, before an event that put 500 trees into the ground. The project was designed by Olga Levari and Trish Heather Hayes, two women who have long made the park their business.

It was part of something larger. That May the foundation had joined a national greening campaign with SUSO, the Kenya Forest Service and the National Youth Council, which planted 30,000 seedlings across more than ten Kenyan towns and cities on a single day and aimed at 400,000 seedlings before the end of June 2021.

Planting is only the beginning of a tree's life. The pattern set here, with young people growing, planting and then tending what they put in the ground, became the way the foundation works with trees wherever it works.

featuredImage.altText: Visitors and community members planting tree seedlings in Nairobi National Park

projects.title: Dignity Housing for wildlife rangers
projects.excerpt: Rangers spend weeks at a time living where the wildlife they protect lives, and for years many did so in tents with no beds, kitchen or bathroom. Since 2021 Dignity Housing has been building them proper homes: self-contained units with beds, a kitchenette, a shower and flush toilet, solar power and water tanks, in Nairobi National Park, Amboseli and Samburu.
projects.content:
Rangers spend weeks at a time living where the wildlife they protect lives. For years, many of them did so in basic tents and worn-out shelters, in the rhino sanctuary of Nairobi National Park and beyond.

The project began in March 2021, with a warden’s idea. Joseph Dadacha, Senior Warden of Nairobi National Park, wanted to replace the small tents that housed the rhino rangers living inside the park’s rhino sanctuary. The tents had no beds, no bathroom and no kitchen. Maniago Safaris, the foundation and Stand Up Shout Out designed and built the first two self-contained container homes together and moved them into the first two rhino blocks, then fitted water tanks, plumbing and solar power so that the rangers had running water, warm showers and electricity. There are twenty-five rhino blocks in the park, and the foundation set out to build a home for every one of them: twenty-five fully fitted homes at US$14,000 each, a programme of US$350,000.

The first two homes were in place by April 2021, a bio-digester dug in beside them and bushes planted around them as camouflage. The third and fourth followed that August. In September 2021 the foundation brought Martin Meyer and prospective donors into the park to see them, and Senior Warden Dadacha explained what these particular rangers do: through their determination, their training and sheer commitment, not one rhino had been poached in Nairobi National Park in over seven years, while the population went on growing with new calves.

The Luigi Footprints Foundation developed Dignity Housing to give these rangers self-contained container homes. Each home has three beds, a small kitchenette, a shower and flush toilet, solar power for lighting and hot water, and large water tanks. The foundation has now built these homes across three landscapes: Amboseli, Nairobi National Park and Samburu National Reserve. Around the homes, the foundation and the rangers plant trees together.

The fifth house was launched there in July 2025, when the Kenya Wildlife Service read a message of appreciation for the partnership between KWS, Maniago Safaris, the foundation and Stand Up Shout Out, and the sixth was handed over to the Rhino Rangers in October 2025.

In October 2025 the work crossed to Samburu National Reserve. After a meeting by the Ewaso Nyiro River between the foundation's Peter Karanja, Honorary Warden Annabella Francescon and Reserve Director Tom Lesarge, ground was broken in November with Tom Lesarge and contractor Benson Omolo, and construction ran through December. The units were donated by trustee Annabella Francescon.

In early 2026 the Governor of Samburu County, H.E. Jonathan Lati Lelelit, officially opened the Samburu Dignity Housing: eight units, a kitchen and washrooms at a bridge crossing that had never had a permanent ranger base. The security point can now be manned, and rangers can respond faster. On World Ranger Day 2026 the foundation returned to plant trees around the homes.

Each fully fitted home costs US$14,000, and twenty-five of them come to US$350,000. If a whole unit is funded, a plaque with your name or the name of your organisation goes onto the home.
